title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
This project set out to explore how quantum computing approaches the Max-Cut problem differently from classical methods. Using Google’s Cirq library, I implemented the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and compared it against brute force and greedy classical baselines across graphs ranging from 4 to 30 nodes.
My six measurable goals were: formulating Max-Cut as an Ising Hamiltonian, implementing QAOA in Cirq, simulating quantum circuits, building classical baselines, evaluating approximation ratios, and analyzing runtime scaling.

QAOA consistently outperformed greedy on smaller graphs but both methods degraded at larger sizes, an expected consequence of p=1 circuit depth.
The most striking result was runtime scaling. At n=30, brute force took 118 minutes while QAOA simulation took ~103 minutes. Projecting forward, brute force would take ~43 years at n=50. On real quantum hardware, that same QAOA circuit would run in microseconds.

title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
Reflection
The hardest part was finding research that explained expected results without giving away the implementation. Significant work constraints — four week-long field projects and a two-week remote dam maintenance assignment — made data collection difficult. The unexpected passing of my last close grandparent added further challenge during the project period.
The most surprising finding was QAOA occasionally losing to greedy. This turned out to be expected behavior at p=1 under classical simulation constraints and is not a flaw in the implementation.

title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
What’s Next
Given more time I would run circuits on real quantum hardware via IBM Quantum, implement higher p values to show quality improvement with circuit depth, and benchmark against the Goemans-Williamson semidefinite programming approach.

title: QAOA Progress: Cut Visualizations
text:
As part of the ongoing QAOA experiments, I have been generating cut visualizations across different graph sizes. For each graph, blue nodes are in partition 1 and red nodes are in partition 0. Green edges cross the partition boundary and contribute to the cut value. Gray edges connect nodes in the same partition and contribute nothing.



At n=8 all three methods achieved an approximation ratio of 1.000, meaning every method found the same maximum cut of 38.43. This confirms the implementations are correct and agree on small graphs.
Graph Structure (n=8)

Brute Force — Cut: 38.43 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 38.43 (ratio: 1.000)

QAOA — Cut: 37.65 (ratio: 0.980)





At n=10 the methods begin to diverge noticeably. Greedy drops to a ratio of 0.839 while QAOA holds at 0.959. This is the first graph size where the choice of algorithm starts to meaningfully affect solution quality.
Graph Structure (n=10)

Brute Force — Cut: 45.77 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 38.40 (ratio: 0.839)

QAOA — Cut: 43.90 (ratio: 0.959)





At n=30 brute force took 118 minutes to find the optimal cut while QAOA simulation took approximately 103 minutes. Both methods are expensive at this scale when run classically. The graph is noticeably more complex and the partition boundaries are harder to visually interpret, which reflects the increased difficulty of the problem.
Graph Structure (n=30)

Brute Force — Cut: 361.54 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 303.28 (ratio: 0.839)

QAOA — Cut: 310.21 (ratio: 0.858)


More analysis and final results coming in the project evaluation post.

title: NoteSearch Part 1: Building a Personal Search Engine in C++
text:
I wanted a fast, private, desktop search tool for my personal notes — something that could scan a folder full of .txt and .md files and surface results by relevance without sending anything to the internet. No Electron, no web server, no cloud. Just a compiled C++ binary that owns its own data.
The core of the project is an inverted index — the same fundamental data structure that powers large-scale search engines. The idea is simple: instead of searching through every file every time a query comes in, you build a map upfront that goes from words to the files they appear in. Lookups then become direct index hits rather than full scans.
The goals for this first phase were:

Build an inverted index from a directory of text files
Support exact and partial (substring) word matching
Implement multi-word AND search with frequency-based scoring
Extract a snippet showing where the term appears in the file
Keep the architecture clean and extensible for future file types

text:
Reflection
The trickiest part was getting the AND search logic right with partial matching in play. Because getFilesForTerm() returns files for both exact and substring hits, a file can satisfy a term match via a substring even if the exact word doesn’t appear. That’s by design, but it’s worth understanding — searching "hash table" could match a file containing "hashtable" and "turntable" even if neither exact word appears independently.
The architecture decision I’m most satisfied with is keeping tokenization shared and consistent. It’s a small thing but eliminates an entire class of subtle bugs where the indexer and search engine would process text differently.

text:
What’s Next
The backend is complete and tested. The next phase is wrapping it in a proper desktop GUI using Qt Widgets — a native Windows application with a directory picker, search bar, and results list, all backed by the same pure C++ engine built here.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
The backend for NoteSearch was complete — a working inverted index, keyword search, scoring, and snippet extraction, all in pure C++. But it lived behind a terminal loop. For a tool I actually want to use every day, that isn’t good enough. This phase was about wrapping that engine in a proper desktop application using Qt Widgets.
The guiding principle throughout was clean separation: the backend knows nothing about Qt, and Qt knows nothing about the indexing logic. The UI is a shell that passes user input in and displays results out. Nothing more.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
The backend for NoteSearch was complete — a working inverted index, keyword search, scoring, and snippet extraction, all in pure C++. But it lived behind a terminal loop. For a tool I actually want to use every day, that isn’t good enough. This phase was about wrapping that engine in a proper desktop application using Qt Widgets.
The guiding principle throughout was clean separation: the backend knows nothing about Qt, and Qt knows nothing about the indexing logic. The UI is a shell that passes user input in and displays results out. Nothing more.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
Why Qt
For a personal desktop tool that lives entirely offline with no web dependencies, the realistic C++ UI options are Qt, wxWidgets, and Dear ImGui. Qt stood out for two reasons. First, it produces genuinely professional-looking native applications on Windows without much effort. Second, Qt is widely used in industry; embedded systems, desktop software, internal tooling makes for a great learning opportunity. The cross platform nature of Qt is a bonus, but Windows is the primary target for this project.
The version used here is Qt 6 with MinGW on Windows, built and managed through Qt Creator and CMake.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
Architecture: The Shell Pattern
The most important decision in this phase wasn’t about UI design — it was about where the boundary between Qt and C++ sits. The rule I set was strict:

Indexer, SearchEngine, and Tokenizer are pure C++ with no Qt includes
MainWindow is the only place Qt lives, and it only calls into the backend through standard C++ interfaces using std::string and std::vector

This means the backend could be dropped into any other frontend — a CLI, a different GUI framework, or a web server — without touching a single line of indexing or search logic. Qt is genuinely just a shell.
The data flow is straightforward:
User action in Qt UI
    → MainWindow converts Qt types to std::string
        → Indexer / SearchEngine does its work
            → Results returned as std::vector
                → MainWindow converts back to Qt types for display
The conversion points are small and explicit. QString::toStdString() going in, QString::fromStdString() coming out. That’s the entire surface area between the two worlds.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
What the UI Does
The interface is intentionally minimal. There are three interactive elements:

A directory input and Browse button that opens a native folder picker and triggers index building
A search input and Search button (also triggered by pressing Enter) that runs a query against the built index
A results list that shows each matching file with its relevance score and a snippet preview

When a directory is selected, the index builds immediately and the results area confirms how many unique terms were found. Searches from that point are fast since the index is already in memory.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
Keeping the Build Clean
Integrating Qt into an existing C++ project required updating the CMake configuration to declare Qt dependencies and tell the compiler where to find the backend headers:
find_package(Qt6 6.5 REQUIRED COMPONENTS Core Widgets)

target_include_directories(SearchEngine PRIVATE
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src
)
The include/ directory holds the backend headers and src/ holds all source files. Keeping them separate makes it visually clear which code belongs to the engine and which belongs to the UI.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
Reflection
The separation of concerns principle paid off immediately during integration. Because the backend had no Qt dependencies, dropping it into the Qt project was straightforward — update CMake, include the headers in MainWindow, and call the same functions that were already working in the terminal version. There was no refactoring of backend logic at all.
The Qt learning curve was real but manageable. Qt Creator’s UI designer makes laying out widgets intuitive, and Qt’s signal and slot system for connecting button clicks to handler functions is clean once the mental model clicks. The trickiest part was getting CMake and Qt Creator to agree on where the source files lived, particularly after reorganizing the project into src/ and include/ subdirectories.

title: NoteSearch Part 2: Adding a Desktop UI with Qt Widgets
text:
What’s Next
The next phase is extending the indexer to support .pdf and .docx files, keeping the same architecture — pure C++ parsers in the backend, no Qt involved in the parsing logic. The UI will surface file type information in the results list once that support is in place.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text: At the end of Part 2, NoteSearch was a functioning desktop application capable of indexing and searching through .txt and .md files. The backend was pure C++, the Qt UI was a clean shell around it, and the two were deliberately kept separate. The natural next step was extending the indexer to handle richer document formats — starting with .docx.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text:
The Challenge with Word Documents
Word documents aren’t a simple text format. A .docx file is actually a ZIP archive containing a collection of XML files. The document content lives inside word/document.xml, wrapped in a hierarchy of XML tags. To extract searchable text, you have to unzip the archive, locate that file, parse the XML, and pull out the text nodes — all before tokenization can even begin.
This required two external libraries: miniz for ZIP extraction and pugixml for XML parsing. Both are pure C++ with no external dependencies, which kept the backend clean and Qt-free.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text:
Integrating the Libraries
Getting miniz and pugixml into the project was more involved than expected. Both libraries ship as multiple files rather than true single-header drops, and the CMake configuration needed explicit source file declarations and language properties to compile the C files correctly in a C++ project. Downloading the full release packages rather than individual files resolved most of the integration friction.
Once the libraries were correctly wired into CMakeLists.txt, the actual DocxParser implementation was straightforward — open the ZIP, locate word/document.xml, extract it into memory, parse the XML with pugixml, walk the <w:t> nodes, and concatenate the text content.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text:
The Application
Here is the main NoteSearch window after indexing a directory containing a mix of .txt, .md, and .docx files:
 
The interface is intentionally minimal consisting of a directory picker, a search bar, and a results list. After selecting a folder the index builds immediately and the result area confirms how many unique terms were found across all supported file types.
Searching across a directory containing both plain text and Word documents returns results from all file types together, ranked by relevance score:



Search results across docx and txt files


Each result shows the file path, its relevance score, and a snippet preview showing where the term appears in the document. The word count index confirms the breadth of what was indexed.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text:
Reflection
The architectural decision to keep the backend Qt-free continued to pay dividends here. Adding an entirely new file format required no changes to the UI, no changes to the search logic, and no changes to the tokenizer. The only new code was the parser itself and a single branch in the indexer.
The library integration was the roughest part of this phase. Working with C libraries inside a C++ CMake project on Windows with MinGW introduced several friction points around file discovery and compilation flags that wouldn’t have been issues on Linux. The lesson is to always download full library releases rather than cherry-picking individual files from a repository.

title: NoteSearch Part 3: Extending the Engine to Word Documents
text:
What’s Next
PDF support is the next planned extension, following the same pattern — a pure C++ PdfParser in the backend, no Qt involvement, same tokenization pipeline. Once both formats are supported the application will cover the full range of personal note formats most people actually use.
